A Hydrogen Evolution Catalyst [Co
2
O
2
] Metallacycle Enables
Regioselective Allene C(sp
2
)-H Functionalization
Yating Liang
+
, Jiayi Feng
+
, Huilong Li, Xiaoli Wang, Ying Zhang, Weigang Fan,
Sheng Zhang,* and Man-Bo Li*
In memory of Professor Xiyan Lu.
Abstract: Selective functionalization of allenic C(sp
2
)-H
is an ideal approach to upgrading simple allenes to
synthetically useful allenes, albeit suffering from chal-
lenges associated with inert reactivity and inferior
selectivity. Inspired by energy chemistry, a catalytic
hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) strategy was
leveraged to selectively activate weakly acidic allene
C(sp
2
)-H bonds in a reductive mode. An array of
[Co
2
O
2
] metallacycle complexes were readily devised
starting from amino acids, and they were demonstrated
as robust HER catalysts, which would selectively break
allenic C(sp
2
)-H bonds to release hydrogen. With the
newly developed HER catalyst, regioselective electro-
chemical functionalization of allenic C(sp
2
)-H with
alcoholic α C(sp
3
)-H was unprecedentedly achieved.
This strategy features excellent regioselectivity, uncon-
ventional chemoselectivity, good functional-group tol-
erance (62 examples), and mild conditions. Mechanism
experiments revealed a reactive hydroxy-coordinated
cobalt(II) species in the reaction. Density functional
theory (DFT) calculations were also conducted to
rationalize the regioselectivity observed in the reaction.
Introduction
Allene is one of the most versatile building blocks and
widely distributed in natural products and
pharmaceuticals.
[1–5]
The functionalization of allenes is an
attractive and direct approach to allene derivatization
(Figure 1A). Although the hydrofunctionalization of al-
lenes pioneered by Krische
[6–11]
has been well-documented,
the direct functionalization of allenic C(sp
2
)-H bonds still
suffers from some challenging issues in the transformation
associated with the inert reactivity and inferior selectivity.
To circumvent these issues, activated allenes bearing
electron-withdrawing groups
[12–17]
or 1,1-disubstituted
allenes
[18–19]
are commonly required in the previous reports.
Recently, Wang
[20]
elegantly developed a strategy to
enhance the acidity of simple allenes using a cationic
cyclopentadienyliron catalyst (Figure 1B). Almost at the
same time, Carreira
[21]
group unveiled a palladium-cata-
lyzed allene C � H functionalization with the assistance of a
picolinamide directing group (Figure 1C). Very recently,
remarkable progress in the selective cyanation of allenic
C(sp
2
)-H has been independently achieved by Liu
[22]
and
Wu
[23]
through a copper-catalyzed radical relay strategy
(Figure 1D). Despite the prominent achievements, these
approaches involve sophisticated catalysts, stoichiometric
oxidants, or high temperatures; a general and mild
approach is still in high demand. As a part of our
continuous interests in exploring the potential of electro-
chemistry in organic synthesis,
[24–29]
we envisaged that
synthetic electrochemistry
[30–40]
might offer an alternative
solution for this transformation.
Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER)
[41–46]
is one of the
most fundamental transformations that convert energy
from electricity into fuels. The development of HER
catalysts featuring high efficiency and availability would
significantly revolutionize energy storage and delivery
systems, and tremendous progress has been achieved.
Moreover, drawing inspiration from catalytic HER would
bring changes to the challenges in synthetic chemistry.
Recently, Baran
[47]
and Lin
[48]
independently reported
electrochemical protocols to intercept cobalt hydride spe-
cies in cobalt-catalyzed HER. Nevertheless, using HER
catalysts to leverage organic transformations directly still
received far less attention. From the perspective of organic
synthesis, HER provides a reductive activation mode for
allenic C(sp
2
)-H by shifting its dissociation equilibrium;
allenyl carbanions
[49]
would be generated in high regiose-
lective control, thus facilitating their selective functionali-
zation (Figure 1E). Discovering a simple and efficient HER
catalyst is critical for the success of the electrochemical
transformations.
In previous reports, DuBois and co-workers
[50]
demon-
strated that amine base sites as proton relays in HER
catalyst could significantly improve its catalytic perform-
ance (Figure 1F). Inspired by the work, [Co
2

2

cycle complexes of amino acids containing multiple base

catalysts (Figure 1F). Although the μ-OH bridged binu-
clear cobalt(III) complexes have been investigated in
coordination chemistry,
[51–52]
their HER catalytic perform-
ance remains elusive. In this work, these readily available
and scalable complexes showed robust HER catalytic
activity and provided a mild avenue for allenyl carbanions.
By virtue of the novel catalyst and a cocatalyst 2,2,6,6-
tetramethylpiperidoxyl (TEMPO),
[53]
electrochemical func-
tionalization of allenic C(sp
2
)-H with alcohols was readily
achieved in high regioselectivity and unconventional che-
moselectivity (Figure 1G), which previously only afford
O � C coupling
[54–55]
and hydrofunctionalization
[6–11]
products.
This electrochemical protocol exhibits some impressive
advantages: a) simple catalyst; b) unconventional regio-
and chemoselectivity; c) good functional-group tolerance
(62 examples); d) mild conditions.
Results and Discussion
C atalyst synthesis and electrocatalytic performance
investigation
According to the previous reports,
[51–52]
we prepared a
broad range of [Co

O
2

procedure involving deprotonation, coordination, and in
situ air oxidation (Figure 2A). Further centrifugation and
evaporation of the reaction mixture gave purified products
by removing KCl precipitate. The [Co

O
2
] metallacycle
structure was unambiguously identified by the single crystal
diffraction of cat 2.
[56]
As shown in Figure 2B, the [Co

metallacycle core is composed of μ-OH bridged binuclear
cobalt(III) centers, which endows the catalyst with alkalin-

substrates. The catalyst structure was further characterized
by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and liquid
phase mass spectrum (LC-MS) (Figure S2–S17).

Reaction optimization and substrate scope examination
With the promising HER catalytic performance of the
[Co
2
O
2

electrochemical functionalization of allene 1 a, which con-

benzyl alcohol, 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidoxyl (TEMPO)
was introduced as a cocatalyst in the paired electrolysis
system. To our delight, a regioselective product 3 a was
exclusively observed in 80 % yield by using cat 1 as HER
catalyst, DMF as solvent,

as the structurally similar L-Valine catalyst (cat 2) gave a
comparable yield (Entry 2). Replacing [Co
2
O
2
] metalla-
cycle catalysts with a conventional HER catalyst (cat 8) led
to significantly diminished yield (30 %, Entry 8), suggesting
the superiority of the newly developed catalysts. To
demonstrate the crucial role of amine sites in the catalyst,
cat 9 and cat 10 were investigated in the reaction, and
product 3 a was delivered in trace and 39 % yield,
respectively (Entries 9–10). This experimental observation
supports the necessity of amine sites in the catalyst. The
control experiment removed either HER catalyst (cat 1) or
TEMPO shut down the reaction directly (Entry 11). Under
the optimal conditions, we quantified the byproduct hydro-
gen released from the reaction with a GC analysis (Fig-
ure S39), and around 0.51 mmol hydrogen was determined
to support the acceptorless dehydrogenation process.
Having identified the optimal conditions, we turned our
attention to examining substrate generality (Scheme 1). A
broad range of alcohol substrates were employed in the
electrochemical protocol. Initially, we investigated the
electronic effect by using para-substituted benzyl alcohols.
It was found that electron-donating groups (3 a–3 h) were
favored in the reaction compared with electron-withdraw-
ing ones (3 i–3 o), presumably due to their lower oxidation
potential. We replaced cat 1 with cat 2 to overcome the
inertness of the electron-deficient substrates. Subsequently,
the superiority of our protocol was further demonstrated
with some challenging but useful functional groups such as
thioether (3 p), vinyl (3 q), amine (3 r), iodine (3 s), carbox-
ylate (3 t) and boric ester (3 u); corresponding products
were readily observed albeit with lower yields. The
hydrolysis of ester groups induced by the alkalinity of
allenyl carbanions gives rise to deteriorated yields (3 t–3 u).
Other substitution patterns (3 v–3 z), fused rings (3 aa–3 ad),
and heterocycles (3 ae–3 af) were tested with the optimal
conditions, and largely maintained yields were observed.
Furthermore, aliphatic alcohols (3 ag–3 ak) were also found
to be suitable substrates to deliver desired products with
synthetically useful yields (30–73 %). Specifically, cyclo-
propylmethanol affords the desired product 3 ag in 73 %
without detecting radical-initiated ring expansion product,
suggesting a possible ionic pathway. This electrochemical
approach enables a platform for the late-stage functionali-
zation of the pharmaceutical Adapalene-derived alcohol
(3 al). Remarkably, our approach could readily discriminate
two alcoholic α C � H bonds to give the site-selective
products 3 am–3 an. Nevertheless, secondary alcohols failed
to afford the desired products.
To further illustrate the generality of the electrochem-
ical protocol, various allenes were synthesized and tested in
the reaction. As shown in Scheme 2, changing aliphatic
chain R to other groups (3 ao–3 as) marginally affected the
reaction yield. Notably, allene bearing a cyclopropyl group
was employed to probe the reaction mechanism, and the
desired product 3 ar was afforded in 75 % yield. Investiga-
tion on the allene substitution revealed that 1,1-disubsti-
tuted allene (3 at) and trisubstituted allene (3 au) were
amenable to afford the desired products, albeit with lower
yields. The electronic effect (3 av–3 bd) and position of
substituents (3 be–3 bf) were next explored. In general, this
electrochemical approach showed good tolerance for these
variations, and corresponding products were accessed in
satisfactory yields. We also tested the site selectivity of the
reaction using an allyloxy substituted allene, and the allenic
C(sp
2
)-H functionalization product 3 bg was exclusively
accessed. Substrates containing naphthyl (3 bh) or thienyl
(3 bi–3 bj) groups proceeded smoothly in the reaction to
give desired allenol products. Alkyl disubstituted allenes
and tertiary butyl allene proved unsuccessful substrates
due to their weak acidity or steric hindrance.
Applications in synthesis and mechanism investigation
The synthetic utility of our protocol was next explored with
the direct derivatization of 3 a (Figure 3A). Interestingly,
two types of dehydrated products 4 and 5 were selectively
accessed. In the presence of trimethyl phosphate, a
conjugated enyne product 4 was accessed in 66 %. On the
contrary, using a catalytic Lewis acid AuCl
3
led to a
cyclized product 5 via a Fridel-Crafts type reaction.
To shed light into the reaction mechanism, a cyclic
voltammetry (CV) study, control experiments, and calcu-
lations were conducted. First, CV revealed that the anodic
oxidation of benzyl alcohol was mediated by TEMPO with
the detection of an obvious catalytic current (Figure S28).

It shows that the allenic
C(sp
2
)-H bond cleavage might be the rate-determining step
in the reaction (Figure 3D). Finally, we conducted various
control experiments to ascertain the real reactive catalyst
in the reaction (Figure 3E). Using stoichiometric cat 1
directly shut down the reaction in the absence of electricity
(Eq. g). Replacing cat 1 with in situ formed Co(II) species
A affords the desired product 3 a in 64 % yield (Eq. h),
whereas species B fails to give any product (Eq. i). These
observations are consistent with the results of CV experi-
ment (Figure 2E); the species A is identified as the real
catalytic species, while B and precatalyst cat 1 are inactive
species in the reaction.
On the basis of the mechanism studies and related
reports,
[41–48]
we proposed a plausible reaction mechanism
(Figure 3F). Under cathodic reduction, [Co
2
O
2
] metalla-
cycle cat 1 is initially converted to cobalt(II) species A and
B. As mentioned earlier, A is the real reactive species that
could promote the dissociation of 1 a to afford carbanion D
and a water-coordinated Co(II) complex C. Subsequently,
a single electron transfer (SET) reduction of C generates a
highly active Co(I) species E, which proceeds a subsequent
proton relay to give F. Hydrogen evolution and regener-
ation of A can be accessed through the dimerization of
hydrogen atom in the Co(III) complex F. On the other
hand, benzyl alcohol was readily oxidized to benzaldehyde
G with the mediation of TEMPO. The final product 3 a was
generated via the nucleophilic addition between G and D.
C onclusion
In conclusion, a series of [Co
2
O
2
] metallacycle complexes
were readily synthesized and well characterized. They were
unveiled as robust hydrogen evolution catalysts, allowing a
mild and highly selective reduction approach for allenic
C(sp
2
)-H bonds. Under paired electrolysis, a highly regio-
selective allene C(sp
2
)-H functionalization with alcohols
was unprecedentedly achieved. We rationalized the uncon-
ventional regioselectivity with various control experiments
and DFT calculations. The further application of the
[Co
2
O
2
] metallacycle catalysts has been actively studied in
our laboratory.
